title: Continual Learning for AI Agents: From Failures to Durable Improvements - Soheil Feizi, RELAI

summary: Soheil Feizi introduces continual learning for AI agents: improving them from experience without forgetting prior capabilities. The agent stack has three layers where learning can occur—model (weights), harness (prompts, skills, tools, code, workflow, context), and memory (session or persistent). Two fundamental challenges arise: obtaining feedback and acting on it. Development uses benchmarks with evaluators, but production only yields logs, often without explicit feedback. Feedback on logs comes from automatic critique (scalable) or human experts (alignment-critical). Log-plus-feedback is insufficient because it is not testable, so Feizi argues for inferring replayable learning environments—simulations with defined grading—so candidate agents can be rerun and evaluated. For acting on feedback, the model layer offers SFT, RL post-training (DPO, GRPO, RLVR), and LoRA but needs benchmarks and explicit evaluators. The harness layer includes trace-to-harness approaches (wipe-based, not testable, risk hidden regressions) and testable prompt-search methods like GEPPO. The memory layer (LETA, MemZero, skill distillation) is cheapest and fastest but usually unverified. A good learning engine should seek the smallest durable change at the right layer. Feizi proposes verifiable continual learning (VCL): every fix proven to help and proven to break nothing that already worked, via executable tests, measured deltas, and regression tests. Four principles govern this: replayability (turn one-off failures into rerunnable tests), holisticness (route fixes to the right layer), lifelongness (new fixes must not regress past behavior via regression-aware optimization treating regression within the loop, not post-hoc), and efficiency (the loop must run frequently; changes vary in cost from cheap memory writes to expensive weight updates; complexity must not scale linearly with the number of past environments K). RELAI's VCL engine implements this loop: signals (logs, feedback, instructions) are lifted into replayable learning environments, root cause analysis routes fixes to the right layer, regression-aware optimization ensures no regressions, and the loop runs efficiently, outputting a reviewable version update. Integration requires just two commands after a one-time setup. Feizi demonstrates on a fictional support-agent benchmark with regression traps: creating a learning environment from an instruction about rude/adversarial callers yields an initial score of 78%, and one optimization loop improves the average by 10%, raising the score to 97% from 87%. A second demo shows lifting a production log with feedback into a replayable environment and optimizing without regression. He concludes with three takeaways: continual learning is not necessarily model fine-tuning; production logs are not learning environments; the frontier is regression-aware continual improvement. VCL is available at rely.ai.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Continual learning for agents is not necessarily model fine-tuning; many useful updates happen at the harness and memory layers.
Production logs are not learning environments; they must be transformed into replayable learning environments with defined grading to make fixes testable and verifiable.

Three agent layers can be updated—model, harness, memory—each with different cost, flexibility, and verifiability tradeoffs; a good learning engine seeks the smallest durable change at the right layer.
Verifiable continual learning requires every fix to be proven to help and proven to break nothing that already worked, via executable tests, measured deltas, and regression tests.

Four principles govern practical VCL: replayability, holisticness, lifelongness (regression-aware optimization treating regression within the loop, not post-hoc), and efficiency (frequent, scalable updates).

RELAI's VCL engine lifts signals into replayable environments, routes fixes via root cause analysis, applies regression-aware optimization, and outputs reviewable version updates; integration takes two commands after one-time setup.
The frontier is regression-aware continual improvement: when fixing new failures, the system verifies old capabilities are not forgotten.
VCL compounds over time, enabling lifelong improvement where each update is tested, every gain is measured, and nothing that already works breaks.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Feizi introduces himself and RELAI, framing continual learning as enabling agents to learn from experience by acting, getting feedback, and improving without forgetting.

sections.title: Big Picture and Fundamental Challenges
sections.summary: Agents interact with diverse users, tools, and data; learning can occur at model, harness, or memory layers. Two core challenges: obtaining feedback and acting on it appropriately.

sections.title: Where Feedback Comes From
sections.summary: Development uses benchmarks with evaluators; production only has logs. Feedback on logs comes automatically (model/LLM critique, scalable) or from human experts (lower volume, alignment-critical). Log-plus-feedback is insufficient because it is not testable.

sections.title: Replayable Learning Environments
sections.summary: A replayable learning environment infers a distribution from one observation, simulating tools, synthetic users, and evaluators so candidate agents can be rerun and evaluated, making fixes testable and verifiable.

sections.title: Acting on Feedback: Three Layers
sections.summary: Model layer (SFT, RL post-training, LoRA) is expensive; harness layer (prompts, skills, tools, code) offers flexibility; memory layer stores facts and skills cheaply. Good learning seeks the smallest durable change at the right layer.

sections.title: Model-Layer Methods
sections.summary: SFT imitates correct trajectories; RL methods like DPO, GRPO, RLVR reinforce winners; LoRA limits parameter changes for cheaper, safer updates. These need benchmarks and explicit evaluators.

sections.title: Harness- and Memory-Layer Methods
sections.summary: Trace-to-harness is wipe-based and risks regressions; GEPPO/prompt search is testable but needs benchmarks. Memory methods (LETA, MemZero, skill distillation) are cheapest and fastest but usually unverified.

sections.title: Verifiable Continual Learning and Principles
sections.summary: Introduces verifiable continual learning with executable tests, measured deltas, and regression tests. Begins four principles: replayability, holisticness, lifelongness (regression-aware learning), and an efficiency principle being introduced as the section ends.

sections.title: Efficiency Principle and Four Principles Summary
sections.summary: Completes the efficiency principle: the continual learning loop must run frequently, with cost varying from cheap memory writes to expensive weight updates; regression-aware optimization treats regression within the loop, not post-hoc; complexity must not scale linearly with K. Summarizes the four principles: replayability, holisticness, lifelongness, efficiency.

sections.title: RELAI's VCL Engine and Integration
sections.summary: Describes RELAI's learning loop: signals (logs, feedback, instructions) are lifted into replayable learning environments, root cause analysis routes fixes to the right layer, regression-aware optimization ensures no regressions, and the loop runs efficiently, outputting a reviewable version update. Integration requires a one-time setup plus two commands.

sections.title: Demo: Fictional Support-Agent Benchmark
sections.summary: Demonstrates VCL on a fictional support-agent benchmark with deterministic evaluators and regression traps. An instruction about rude/adversarial callers generates a learning environment with personas, intents, tools, and evaluators. Initial score is 78%; one optimization loop yields 10% average improvement, raising the score to 97% from 87%.

sections.title: Demo: Production Log with Feedback
sections.summary: Shows lifting a production log with feedback ('keep fast eligible refunds, but do not generalize generosity beyond refund thresholds') into a replayable learning environment and optimizing without regressing past behavior, demonstrating compounding lifelong improvement.

sections.title: Key Takeaways and Conclusion
sections.summary: Three takeaways: continual learning is not necessarily model fine-tuning; production logs are not learning environments; the frontier is regression-aware continual improvement. VCL is built on four principles and is available at rely.ai.

demonstrations: Fictional support-agent benchmark with deterministic evaluators and regression traps: an instruction about rude/adversarial callers generates a learning environment with personas, intents, mock/real tools, and evaluators; initial score 78%, one optimization loop yields 10% average improvement, score rises to 97% from 87%.

Production log demo: a support-agent session with feedback ('keep fast eligible refunds, but do not generalize generosity beyond refund thresholds') is lifted into a replayable learning environment and optimized without regressing past behavior.
limitations: Trace-to-harness approaches are wipe-based: effectiveness is unknown even for the target sample, and impact on other scenarios is untested, risking hidden regressions.
Memory-layer updates are usually unverified, with no way to test whether writing to memory resolves the issue or causes regressions.
Model-layer methods (SFT, RL post-training) usually require benchmarks and explicit evaluators and cannot be applied directly to log-plus-feedback without conversion to replayable environments.
Regression-aware optimization complexity must not scale linearly with the number of past learning environments K, as K can grow large.
Benchmarks with regression traps can cause optimizers that overfit to the latest fix to break previously successful behaviors.
